relevance_reason: Reports the second family with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by a homozygous COL9A3 loss-of-function mutation.

findings.statement: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy, born to third-cousin parents from India, with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome. He failed his newborn hearing screen. At 5 months, testing showed moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe loss on the left; the hearing loss stayed stable. A temporal bone CT showed mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months but had high myopia by 2 years (-6.75 OD, -8 OS), which progressed to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS by 12 years. No vitreous abnormalities were noted.
quotes: Audiology evaluation at 5 months identified moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right from 250 through 4,000 Hz and severe sensorineural hearing loss on the left from 250 through 4,000 Hz.
However, by 2 years, he had developed myopia of −6.75 OD and −8 OS. By 12 years, this had progressed to −10.75 OD and −11.25 OS. No vitreous abnormalities have been noted.
The parents of the patient are third cousins from India.

phenotypes.text: sensorineural hearing loss, moderate to severe

findings.statement: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) noted femoral and tibial bowing at birth in their patient. Radiographs at age 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, flattened acetabula, irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly with irregular vertebral endplates. Growth and intelligence were normal, and he did not have cleft palate or pes planus. He also had midfacial hypoplasia and autoimmune hypothyroidism, which was diagnosed at 10 years.
quotes: Femoral and tibial bowing were noted at birth. Radiographs at 6 years demonstrated slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, normal knee epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly (Figure 1). Growth parameters have been in the normal range.
The patient also had autoimmune hypothyroidism that was identified at 10 years.
In addition, he had mild platyspondyly with irregularities of the vertebral endplates.

findings.statement: In the proband from consanguineous family R08-308, Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous single-base duplication in exon 13 of the COL9A3 gene (c.650dupC, NM_001853.3). The frameshift was predicted to cause premature termination and absence of the gene product. The variant was not found in public SNP databases. Sanger sequencing confirmed that both parents and an unaffected sib were heterozygous.
quotes: exome sequencing was used to identify homozygosity for single base duplication c.650dupC in exon 13 of COL9A3 (RefSeq accession number NM_001853.3) of the proband.
The frameshift mutation predicts premature termination of translation and absence of the COL9A3 gene product. The nucleotide change was not found in public SNP databases
Genotyping of the parents and an unaffected sibling showed that all of them were heterozygous for the sequence change (Figure 2).

findings.statement: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) noted that all Stickler syndrome patients with type IX collagen defects had high myopia, midface hypoplasia, and hearing loss ranging from mild to severe. Vitreous and retinal degeneration had been reported with COL9A1 and COL9A2 mutations but not with COL9A3 mutations. The authors suggested that loss of the alpha-3 chain of type IX collagen causes a phenotype similar to the other autosomal recessive type IX collagen forms.
quotes: All of the Stickler syndrome patients with type IX collagen defects have exhibited high myopia, midface hypoplasia, and mild–severe hearing loss. Vitreous and retinal degeneration have been reported in patients with mutations in COL9A1 and COL9A2, but have not been reported in patients with mutations in COL9A3.

We suggest that loss of the α3 chain of type IX collagen results in a Stickler syndrome phenotype similar to that of the other autosomal recessive forms caused by mutations in the genes encoding the α1 and α2 chains of type IX collagen.

relevance_reason: First report of autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by a COL9A3 loss-of-function mutation; this establishes STL6.

findings.statement: In a family with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome, Faletra et al. (2014) identified a loss-of-function mutation in the COL9A3 gene, a 23-bp deletion (c.1176_1198del) that causes a frameshift (p.Gln393Cysfs*25). They described this as the first autosomal recessive Stickler family due to COL9A3 mutation.
quotes: Here, we describe the first autosomal recessive Stickler family due to loss of function mutations (c.1176_1198del, p.Gln393Cysfs*25) of COL9A3 gene.

findings.statement: Faletra et al. (2014) noted that Stickler syndrome is a clinically variable and genetically heterogeneous syndrome with ophthalmic, articular, orofacial, and auditory manifestations. It shows both autosomal dominant inheritance (COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2) and recessive inheritance (COL9A1, COL9A2).
quotes: Stickler syndrome (STL) is a clinically variable and genetically heterogeneous syndrome characterized by ophthalmic, articular, orofacial, and auditory manifestations.
while recessive forms have been associated with mutations of COL9A1 (OMIM 120210) and COL9A2 (OMIM 120260) genes.

relevance_reason: Reports a new patient with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by compound heterozygous COL9A3 nonsense variants, including clinical, radiographic, and segregation data.

findings.statement: Markova et al. (2021) described a boy, born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents, with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome. At 1 month he had hip dysplasia and bilaterally absent ossification centers. At 3 months he had congenital high bilateral myopia. At 11 months he was diagnosed with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss grade 3-4. Ophthalmic findings included peripheral pigment rearrangement, multiple vitreous floaters, a preretinal membrane, and congenital progressive high myopia; the ERG was normal. Radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with platyspondyly, kyphosis, sacral spina bifida occulta, flattened irregular femoral heads, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses.
quotes: At the age of 3 months, a systemic skeletal disease was suspected at the orthopedic examination and ophthalmologic examination showed congenital high bilateral myopia.
At the age of 11 months, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss grade 3–4 was diagnosed by a surdologist, and hearing‐aids were assigned.
The US showed multiple vitreous floaters OU, OS>OD, OD preretinal membrane growth (9 mm) in the posterior chamber. The ophthalmologist diagnosed OU congenital progressive high myopia.

findings.statement: Markova et al. (2021) examined the proband at age 2 years 5 months. He had valgus knee deformity, waddling gait, fatigability, and pain in the lower limb joints from age 3 years, which the authors took as indicating early-onset arthropathy. Height was normal. He had a flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, and high palate, without cleft palate. The authors concluded that he had a more severe phenotype than previously reported COL9A3 patients, with early-onset arthropathy and vitreoretinal degeneration.
quotes: Several dysmorphic facial features were presented with a slightly flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild mid‐facial hypoplasia, high palate.
The height is within the average range, but the pain in lower limb joints developing from the age of 3 years indicates early‐onset arthropathy.
Our case further expands the known phenotype with a more severe clinical presentation of an early‐onset arthropathy and vitreoretinal degeneration.

findings.statement: Markova et al. (2021) used targeted sequencing of 166 skeletal disorder genes in the proband and identified compound heterozygous nonsense variants in the COL9A3 gene: c.268C>T (p.Arg90Ter) in exon 5 and c.1729C>T (p.Arg577Ter) in exon 30. Sanger sequencing of the parents showed that the variants were in trans, and the healthy sibs did not carry pathogenic variants. The authors described this as the first COL9A3-related recessive Stickler case caused by compound heterozygous rather than homozygous loss-of-function variants.
quotes: Targeted sequencing of 166 genes associated with congenital skeletal disorders identified two undescribed heterozygous nucleotide variants in the COL9A3 gene: c.268C>T (p.Arg90Ter) in exon 5, and c.1729C>T (p.Arg577Ter) in exon 30.
Segregation analysis of the identified variants in the family by Sanger sequencing showed their trans‐position.
Moreover, we present the first clinical case not caused by a homozygous mutation with two novel compound‐heterozygous LoF mutations.

findings.statement: Markova et al. (2021) compared their patient with 6 previously reported patients from 3 families with homozygous COL9A3 variants. In all of these patients, the reported variants caused loss of function. High myopia and sensorineural hearing loss were present in all cases, and cleft palate and retinal detachment were absent in all. The authors suggested that the absence of cleft palate may distinguish recessive COL9A3-related Stickler syndrome from autosomal dominant forms.
quotes: All the described mutations have led to the loss of function (LoF).

Congenital high myopia and moderately severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss from a very early age were uniform manifestations for all COL9A3 recessive STL patients, including the one in the present study.

All the described COL9A3 recessive STL cases were characterized by the absence of cleft palate, possibly being a hallmark of autosomal dominant STL forms where this trait is noted in 41% of cases [3].

relevance_reason: The paper reports three consanguineous Iranian families with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by novel homozygous loss-of-function variants in COL9A3 (STL6).

findings.statement: Rad et al. (2022) described a 28-year-old Iranian woman (family 1), the only affected child of first-cousin parents, who had high myopia in both eyes, vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations and retinal pigmentary changes, and severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Skull x-ray showed unilateral absence of the frontal sinus. Examination of her joints and bones was normal, but she complained of knee pain. Typical Stickler craniofacial features, including midface hypoplasia, cleft palate, micrognathia, depressed nasal bridge and anteverted nares, were absent. Her height was 157 cm (-0.8 SD).
quotes: She suffers from high myopia in both eyes, in addition to vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations and retinal pigmentary changes. There was unilateral absence of the frontal sinus in her skull X-ray. She has severe and progressive sensorineural hearing loss.
X-ray and detailed examination of her joints and bones, including mobility testing and examination for signs of osteoarthritis were normal, however she complained of pain in her knee joints.
Typical STL craniofacial features such as midface hypoplasia, cleft palate, micrognathia, depressed nasal bridge and anteverted nares are absent.

findings.statement: Rad et al. (2022) described 2 affected brothers, aged 65 and 57 years, from an Iranian family (family 2) with first-cousin parents. Both had a history of multiple vitreoretinal surgeries for recurrent rhegmatogenous retinal detachments caused by advanced vitreoretinal degeneration. The older brother was blind with no light perception in either eye. Both had severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss (profound in Table 1), high myopia, cataract and a herniated cervical disc. The older brother also had muscular atrophy.
quotes: Both had a history of multiple vitreoretinal surgeries due to recurrent rhegmatogenous retinal detachments resulting from advanced vitreoretinal degeneration.

Despite vitreoretinal surgeries, the older patient is considered blind without light perception (NLP) in either eye while his sibling has counting finger vision for one eye while NLP was noted for the other eye.
Both suffer from severe and progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Likewise, both show a herniated cervical disc and muscular atrophy was noted in the older sibling.

findings.statement: Rad et al. (2022) described 2 affected sibs, a boy aged 11.8 years and his sister aged 3.1 years, from an Iranian family (family 3) with first-cousin parents. Both had myopia and congenital moderate to severe progressive sensorineural hearing impairment, and x-rays showed spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. Both had pes planus, a depressed nasal bridge and anteverted nares; midface hypoplasia and downslanting palpebral fissures were more pronounced in the girl. The boy had knee pain, genu valgum, irregular femoral epiphyses, a flat acetabular roof, flattened femoral heads and short metacarpals. None of the patients in the 3 families had intellectual disability.
quotes: Both affected individuals have myopia and congenital moderate to severe progressive sensorineural hearing impairment. The affected male complains of knee joint pain, especially when he runs. X-ray and detailed examination demonstrated spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia in both children.
Both individuals II1 and II4 have pes planus, depressed nasal bridge and anteverted nares, with midface hypoplasia and downslanting palpebral fissures more pronounced in II4.
None of the individuals showed signs of intellectual disability.

findings.statement: In the proband of family 1 with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome, Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous 10-bp deletion in exon 2 of the COL9A3 gene (c.107_116del, NM_001853.3), predicted to cause a frameshift (Pro36ArgfsTer49). Segregation was checked by Sanger sequencing in available family members. The variant was found in gnomAD at an allele frequency of 0.00001390 (2 carriers) and was not reported in Iranome, GME or 1000 Genomes.
quotes: The proband in Family 1 was found to have a COL9A3 deletion (c.107_116del, p.(Pro36Argfs*49), rs1470627424), causing a frameshift in exon 2.
The allele frequency in gnomAD is 0.00001390 with two carriers, while other public genomic databases such as Iranome and GME, and 1000 genomes have not reported this variant.
Segregation analysis using Sanger sequencing was performed in available family members to confirm variant segregation after PCR amplification.

findings.statement: In 2 affected brothers from family 2 with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome, Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing of the proband to identify a homozygous nonsense variant in exon 23 of the COL9A3 gene (c.1204C>T, p.Arg402Ter). The variant had not been reported in public databases.
quotes: The proband in family 2 disclosed a COL9A3 nonsense variant (c.1204C > T, p.(Arg402*), rs989413835) in exon 23
Both variants have not been reported in public databases.

findings.statement: In 2 affected sibs from family 3 with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome, Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing of the proband to identify a homozygous 1-bp deletion in exon 7 of the COL9A3 gene (c.355delC), predicted to cause a frameshift (Leu119SerfsTer9; given as fs*10 in Table 1). The variant had not been reported in public databases.
quotes: the proband in Family 3 showed a one base pair deletion in COL9A3 [c.355delC, p.(Leu119Serfs*9)] in exon 7. Both variants have not been reported in public databases.

findings.statement: Reviewing their 3 families and 4 previously reported families with biallelic COL9A3 loss-of-function variants, Rad et al. (2022) found that moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate-to-high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration were consistent features. Retinal detachment and cataract occurred occasionally, and skeletal involvement was more variable. The older patients in family 2 had milder skeletal findings than the young sibs in family 3. Unlike Nixon et al., the authors did not see mild phenotypes in heterozygous carriers.
quotes: Consistent clinical features among STL patients with biallelic COL9A3 LOF alleles comprise moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration. Retinal detachment and cataract occur occasionally. In contrast, skeletal involvement seems to be more variable.
Moreover, Nixon et al. [13] observed that carrier parents can manifest mild STL phenotypes, while our report and others have not observed mild phenotypes in heterozygous individuals.
We find high myopia and moderate-severe hearing loss to be consistent features amongst all cases while skeletal findings seem more variable.

findings.statement: Rad et al. (2022) found that homozygous loss-of-function variants in COL9A3 caused autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome (type VI) in 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families.
quotes: Here, we report three families with five affected individuals clinically diagnosed with autosomal recessive STL due to biallelic LOF variants in COL9A3.
In summary, our report consolidates that homozygous loss of function variants in COL9A3 cause STL (type VI).

relevance_reason: Reports a family with recessive Stickler syndrome caused by homozygous COL9A3 variants (2 patients), plus COL9A1/COL9A2 families, expanding the phenotype.

findings.statement: Nixon et al. (2019) described 6 patients from 4 families with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome due to homozygous variants in type IX collagen genes, including 1 family with 2 affected patients with COL9A3 variants. All patients were highly myopic with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss; 1 patient had severe arthropathy.
quotes: Six affected patients were identified from four pedigrees with variants in COL9A1 (one family, one patient), COL9A2 (two families, three patients), and COL9A3 (one family, two patients).
All patients were highly myopic with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss. One patient had severe arthropathy.

findings.statement: In 2 affected patients from 1 family with recessive Stickler syndrome, Nixon et al. (2019) identified a homozygous variant in the COL9A3 gene; across the 4 families studied (COL9A1, COL9A2, COL9A3), 3 of the variants were novel.
quotes: Six affected patients were identified from four pedigrees with variants in COL9A1 (one family, one patient), COL9A2 (two families, three patients), and COL9A3 (one family, two patients). Three variants were novel.

findings.statement: Nixon et al. (2019) noted that congenital megalophthalmos and myopia are common to dominant and recessive forms of Stickler syndrome, whereas sensorineural hearing loss is more common and severe in recessive Stickler syndrome due to type IX collagen variants.
quotes: Congenital megalophthalmos and myopia are common to dominant and recessive forms of SS. Sensorineural hearing loss is more common and severe in recessive SS.

findings.statement: Nixon et al. (2019) suggested that COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3 be added to genetic screening panels for patients with congenital hearing loss, given the impact of early diagnosis for children with potential dual sensory impairment.
quotes: We suggest that COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3 be added to genetic screening panels for patients with congenital hearing loss.

relevance_reason: Canine animal model: a COL9A3 frameshift insertion causes autosomal recessive oculoskeletal dysplasia (drd1) in Labrador retrievers. The authors propose it as a model for recessive Stickler syndrome.

findings.statement: Goldstein et al. (2010) studied oculoskeletal dysplasia (OSD), which segregates as an autosomal recessive trait in Labrador retriever dogs (locus drd1) and Samoyed dogs (locus drd2). Affected pups were recognizable from about 4 to 6 weeks of age by excessive doming of the cranium, a pronounced facial stop, exotropic strabismus, and short-limbed dwarfism with forelimb curvature and varus/valgus deformity. Eye examination showed radial cortical equatorial cataracts, vitreal liquefaction and frequent complete retinal detachment. The authors noted that the phenotype resembles human arthro-ophthalmopathies such as Stickler syndrome.
quotes: Affected dogs have skeletal abnormalities characterized by short-limbed dwarfism and ocular defects including vitreous dysplasia, retinal detachment and cataracts, and this phenotype segregates as an autosomal recessive trait in both breeds.
The earliest and most easily recognized sign in such pups was an excessive doming of the cranium, together with a more pronounced facial stop and moderate exotropic strabismus.
Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed a range of defects, the most consistent of which were radial cortical equatorial cataracts, and vitreal liquefaction.

findings.statement: Goldstein et al. (2010) found that dogs heterozygous for either drd1 or drd2 had a normal skeleton but could show a mild eye phenotype of retinal folds and vitreal strands. In Labrador-derived litters, 14 of 34 obligate heterozygotes had retinal folds. Retinal folds were not linked to the COL9A3 locus, and 18 Labradors with retinal folds were wildtype at that locus. The authors suggested a possible semidominant mechanism, with haploinsufficiency having an effect in the vitreous but not in cartilage.
quotes: In Labrador retriever-derived OSD-informative litters, 14 of 34 obligate heterozygotes had retinal folds observed when examined between 6 weeks and 3 months of age and 20 were ophthalmoscopically normal.

ophthalmoscopic findings have suggested a possibly semi-dominant mechanism in which heterozygous dogs, although skeletally normal, can either show no ophthalmoscopic abnormalities or have multiple retinal folds, vitreal membranes or vitreous degeneration.
LINKAGE analysis to evaluate cosegregation of the folds phenotype with the drd1 COL9A3 locus (i.e. the mutation) revealed no significant evidence of linkage

findings.statement: Goldstein et al. (2010) mapped the drd1 locus to the telomeric end of canine chromosome 24 (maximum lod score 3.589 with marker FH2079) in 8 colony families derived from Labrador retrievers. This made COL9A3 a positional candidate gene.
quotes: From drd1–informative (Labrador-derived) pedigrees, a maximum lod score of 3.589 was obtained on chromosome 24 (CFA24) for marker FH2079 at theta = 0.142
These mapping results strongly suggested COL9A2 on CFA15 (5,651,564–5,665,086) and COL9A3 on CFA24 (49,700,412–49,713,993), as positional candidates for drd2 and drd1, respectively

findings.statement: In drd1-affected Labrador retrievers, Goldstein et al. (2010) identified a homozygous 1-bp insertion (G) in exon 1 of COL9A3. The insertion causes a frameshift and a premature stop codon after 48 codons, which affects the COL3 domain. The mutation cosegregated with the disease (lod score 25.889 at theta 0.0): all affected dogs were homozygous and all obligate carriers were heterozygous. Among 59 unrelated Labradors and 19 Labradors with retinal folds, 1 dog was homozygous, and it also had short-limbed dwarfism. The allele frequency was estimated at about 1%, and 78 dogs from 21 other breeds were wildtype.
quotes: Sequence of the PCR products revealed a one-base insertion (guanine) in exon 1 that changes a string of 4 guanines (chr24:49,699,847–49,699,850, CanFam2;) to a string of 5 guanines. This shifts the reading frame and introduces a premature stop codon after 48 codons.
All outbred normal dogs were homozygous for the 4 Gs haplotype, all affected dogs were homozygous for the insertion (5 Gs), and all obligate drd1-heterozygotes were heterozygous for the insertion
One dog with retinal folds was found to be homozygous for the mutation. Subsequent enquiry determined that this dog also had orthopedic abnormalities consistent with short-limbed dwarfism.

findings.statement: In Northern blots, Goldstein et al. (2010) found that COL9A3 mRNA (about 3.0 kb) could not be detected in retina from a drd1-affected dog, whereas COL9A2 was still expressed. Because the promoter is not mutated, the authors suggested that nonsense-mediated decay was the likely mechanism.
quotes: only one COL9A3 transcript (approximately 3.0 Kb) is observed in drd1-nonaffected retina (Figure 4B, lanes 1 and 3), and this is absent in a 7.6 weeks old drd1-affected retina
In this case, since the promoter region is not mutated, it is likely that nonsense-mediated-decay is the mechanism responsible.

findings.statement: In drd2-affected Samoyed dogs, Goldstein et al. (2010) identified a homozygous 1,267-bp deletion at the 5-prime end of COL9A2 that removes exon 1. The deletion cosegregated with disease (lod score 23.179). COL9A2 mRNA was absent from affected retina. The authors stated that the canine diseases provide valuable models for the recessive form of Stickler syndrome.
quotes: Sequence analysis of these products revealed a 1,267bp deletion in affected dogs. This mutation deletes all of exon 1 and parts of both the 5′ UTR and intron 1
Nevertheless, these canine diseases provide valuable models for Stickler Syndrome in its recessive mode.

relevance_reason: The paper reports autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by COL9A2 (a different type). For COL9A3 it only mentions canine oculoskeletal dysplasia loci and suggests that loss-of-function mutations in any collagen IX gene, including COL9A3, could cause AR Stickler syndrome.

findings.statement: Baker et al. (2011) described a family with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome with high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, retinal detachment, hearing loss, and short stature. Affected members had a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in COL9A2 (c.843_c.846+4del8). The authors noted that a family with a homozygous loss-of-function COL9A1 mutation had been described before.
quotes: The main clinical findings consisted of high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, retinal detachment, hearing loss, and short stature.
Affected family members were found to have a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in COL9A2, c.843_c.846 + 4del8.

findings.statement: Baker et al. (2011) noted that in dogs with autosomal recessive oculoskeletal dysplasia, a disorder that resembles Stickler syndrome, homozygous loss-of-function mutations in COL9A2 and COL9A3 had been found to co-segregate with the two causative loci.
quotes: In dogs, two causative loci have been identified in autosomal recessive oculoskeletal dysplasia. This dysplasia resembles Stickler syndrome.
Recently, homozygous loss-of-function mutations in COL9A2 and COL9A3 were found to co-segregate with the loci.

findings.statement: Baker et al. (2011) noted that all three collagen IX alpha chains, encoded by COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3, are needed to form a functional collagen IX molecule. They suggested that loss-of-function mutations in any of the collagen IX genes can cause autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome.
quotes: All three collagen IX α chains, α1, α2, and α3, are needed for formation of functional collagen IX molecule.
Together the data from the present study and the previous studies suggest that loss-of-function mutations in any of the collagen IX genes can cause autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome.

relevance_reason: Reports a patient with mild Stickler syndrome caused by a homozygous COL9A3 frameshift variant, identified within a late-onset hearing loss cohort.

findings.statement: Uehara et al. (2022) described a 58-year-old Japanese woman (case 7), born to first-cousin parents, who was diagnosed with hearing loss in her twenties. Her hearing loss was severe in the left ear and moderate in the right, with a flat audiometric pattern. Her older sister also had hearing loss. The patient had no arthritis but had a history of cataract and retinal detachment. The authors classified her as having a very mild type of Stickler syndrome. At first she had been diagnosed with nonsyndromic hearing loss, and the cataract and retinal detachment were found only on re-evaluation after the genetic diagnosis.
quotes: Case 7 is a 58-year-old female, diagnosed with HL in her twenties. Her parents were first cousins and her elder sister also had HL.
This patient did not have any arthritis, but had cataracts and retinal detachment, which are known to be associated with Stickler syndrome.

The present case, the third reported to date, presenting only with HL, cataract and retinal detachment, can be classified as a very mild type of Stickler syndrome that could not be diagnosed without genetic diagnosis.

findings.statement: In a Japanese woman with mild Stickler syndrome whose parents were first cousins, Uehara et al. (2022) identified a homozygous frameshift variant in the COL9A3 gene (c.1587dupT, p.Gly530TrpfsTer71). It was found by massively parallel sequencing of a panel of known deafness genes and confirmed by direct sequencing. The authors classified the variant as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria (PVS1, PM2). It was novel and present at less than 1% in public databases and in in-house Japanese controls.
quotes: Genetic analysis of this patient identified a homozygous COL9A3 gene frame-shift variant (COL9A3: NM_001853:c.1587dupT:p.G530Wfs*71).
Case 7 | COL9A3 | AR | c.1587dupT (homo) | p.G530Wfs*71 | – | – | – | – | – | Likely pathogenic (PVS1, PM2)

findings.statement: Uehara et al. (2022) suggested that COL9A3 variants may cause a broad range of phenotypes, from mild nonsyndromic hearing loss to more severe syndromic forms. They noted that variability between and within families makes clinical diagnosis difficult.
quotes: As COL9A3 variants have been reported to cause non-syndromic HL, COL9A3 variants may have a broad phenotypic range from mild non-syndromic HL to more severe syndromic phenotypes.

relevance_reason: Describes a naturally occurring canine model (Northern Inuit Dog oculoskeletal dysplasia) caused by a homozygous nonsense variant in COL9A3, the gene for Stickler syndrome type VI; animal model evidence only.

findings.statement: Stavinohova et al. (2019) described oculoskeletal dysplasia (OSD) in 7 Northern Inuit Dogs (NID) from 3 related litters in the UK. All affected dogs had short-limbed (disproportionate) dwarfism and angular limb deformities, plus a variable combination of macroglobus, cataracts, lens coloboma, microphakia, and vitreopathy; retinal detachment was present in 5 dogs. Ocular lesions progressed in most dogs to advanced cataract, lens-induced uveitis, posterior lens subluxation, secondary glaucoma, and blindness. Pedigree analysis indicated autosomal recessive inheritance.
quotes: Short-limbed dwarfism, angular limb deformities and a variable combination of macroglobus, cataracts, lens coloboma, microphakia and vitreopathy were present in all seven dogs, while retinal detachment was diagnosed in five dogs.

Ocular lesions progressed in most of the OSD-affected NID to a combination of advanced cataracts (five dogs/10 eyes) associated with visual impairment (two out of 5 dogs/4 eyes), lens induced uveitis (four dogs/eight eyes), posterior lens subluxation (two dogs/four eyes), secondary glaucoma (two dogs/three eyes), and blindness (three dogs/four eyes)
Pedigree analysis revealed that OSD in NID is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

findings.statement: Stavinohova et al. (2019) found by histopathology of an enucleated globe from an affected Northern Inuit Dog a hydrophthalmic globe with lens luxation, cortical cataract, vitreal syneresis, and chronic rhegmatogenous retinal detachment without retinal dysplasia (rosettes); a presumptive diagnosis of vitreoretinopathy was made. Unlike affected Labrador Retrievers, affected NID lacked retinal dysplasia, and heterozygous NID were free of ocular defects.
quotes: Ocular pathology of one globe (Dog 2) (Emma Scurrell, Cytopath Ltd., UK) revealed a hydrophthalmic globe with lens luxation, anterior, equatorial and posterior cortical cataract, vitreal syneresis, chronic rhegmatogenous and retinal detachment.
Retinal dysplasia (rosettes) was not evident within the detached and atrophied retina. A presumptive diagnosis of a vitreoretinopathy was made.
In contrast, all skeletally normal NID, including 14 that were subsequently identified as heterozygotes, were free of ocular defects typical of OSD.

findings.statement: Stavinohova et al. (2019) excluded the known drd1 and drd2 variants and, by whole genome sequencing of 2 affected Northern Inuit Dogs with screening of 9 candidate genes, identified a homozygous nonsense variant in exon 14 of COL9A3 (c.700C>T, p.Arg234Ter) predicted to truncate the protein by 451 amino acids. All 7 affected dogs were homozygous; of 116 unaffected NID, 31 were heterozygous and 85 homozygous wildtype (p = 1.4 x 10(-11)), consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance with complete penetrance. All 1,109 non-NID dogs were homozygous wildtype; allele frequency in NID was 0.08. Retinal COL9A3 mRNA was not reduced in an affected dog, suggesting nonsense-mediated decay may not contribute, though results were inconclusive.
quotes: Based on this, the COL9A3 variant is predicted to be a nonsense SNP (c.700C>T) within a collagen triple helix repeat region (COL3), and to result in a premature termination codon and a protein product truncated by 451 amino acids (p.Arg234Ter) (Fig 6).

Overall, seven OSD-affected NID were homozygous for the variant allele and 116 OSD-unaffected NID were either heterozygous (n = 31) or homozygous for the wildtype allele (n = 85), confirming that the variant is statistically associated with OSD (Fisher’s exact P-value = 1.4x10-11).

Nevertheless, whilst these results are inconclusive, they do suggest that nonsense-mediated decay of the mutated COL9A3 transcript may not contribute to pathogenesis, and if this is the case a truncated protein product is expected to be produced.

relevance_reason: The paper reports autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by a COL9A1 mutation, not COL9A3. It gives context for the STL6 entry: it was the first report of a collagen IX gene causing recessive Stickler syndrome.

findings.statement: Van Camp et al. (2006) reported a consanguineous Moroccan family with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome. The disorder was caused by a homozygous R295X mutation in the collagen IX gene COL9A1, so COL9A1 was the fourth gene identified for Stickler syndrome and the first with recessive inheritance. Four affected children had moderate-to-severe sensorineural hearing loss, moderate-to-high myopia with vitreoretinopathy, and epiphyseal dysplasia. The parents and 4 unaffected sibs were heterozygous carriers without symptoms.
quotes: Mutation analysis of the coding region of the COL9A1 gene showed a homozygous R295X mutation in the four affected children.

Therefore, COL9A1 is the fourth identified gene that can cause Stickler syndrome. In contrast to the three previously reported Stickler syndrome-causing genes, this gene causes a form of Stickler syndrome with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Four children showed symptoms characteristic of Stickler syndrome, including moderate-to-severe sensorineural hearing loss, moderate-to-high myopia with vitreoretinopathy, and epiphyseal dysplasia.
